title: Designing a permission system

facts.text: Authorization sits after authentication, which is assumed done, and is itself a security mechanism that must not be easy to abuse to get around the protection it provides.
The simplest model is an ACL, a list of rules granting or denying users access to a resource: easy to understand, but error-prone with a high maintenance cost.

In DAC the owner decides: an access policy set by the object's owner group grants or restricts access; it is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the owner group has too much power.
In MAC a central policy and classification labels on owners and resources decide access, and users cannot override it; it is strict and straightforward but not flexible.

In RBAC the data model is subjects, roles and permissions with many-to-many assignments: permissions attach to roles, users acquire them only through roles, and a subject can hold several sessions in different roles.

RBAC roles can form a hierarchy in which higher roles subsume permissions of sub-roles, and constraints enforce separation of duties, such as not letting one person both create and authorize an account.
RBAC is flexible in assigning roles and accepted as best practice within a single system, but it can suffer role explosion when finer granularity is needed.
ABAC evaluates attributes of the subject, the action, the resource and the environment through Boolean policy rules; it is flexible, but rules can be complicated and the implementation is hard.

Relationship-based control defines permission by the relationships between subjects and resources, which gives fine-grained permissions, for example in a social network where users share posts with specific other users.
The models combine: RBAC can implement DAC or MAC policies, and ABAC and relationship-based access control build on RBAC.
The check is split into points: a PEP intercepts the request and asks a PDP, which evaluates policies fetched through a retrieval point and gets attributes from information points.

In an API, an interceptor asks the PDP whether Alice can approve transaction 123; the PDP retrieves the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only Permit runs the business logic, otherwise access is denied.
XACML supplies a policy language and request/response scheme, and Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source PDP; the XACML specification does not cover how a PDP is built.
When rules contradict, combining algorithms such as deny-unless-permit or permit-unless-deny resolve the conflict into one final decision.
An obligation tells the PEP what must happen around an approved access, such as logging; if the PEP cannot comply, the approved access may not be realized.

Fine-grained checks cost performance: the more granular the controls, the higher the overhead, and RFC 2904 says the fields for both authentication and authorization SHOULD travel in a single message set to reduce latency.

notes: thin: no source sentence gives the scale of a permission system, concrete requirements, a table-level data model or REST API, caching of permission checks, audit logging or advice on which model to pick; the rationale is assembled from model descriptions and the RFC 2904 and XACML architecture.

definition.text: A list of permissions attached to a system resource that says which users or system processes may access it and which operations they may perform.

facts.text: An ACL specifies which users or system processes are granted or denied access to a resource and which operations are allowed; each entry in a typical ACL names a subject and an operation.
An ACL holding Alice: read, write and Bob: read gives Alice permission to read and write the file and Bob permission only to read it.

A filesystem ACL is a table of access-control entries giving individual users' or groups' rights to specific objects; each object carries an identifier to its ACL, and POSIX and NFSv4 ACLs are usually stored in extended attributes.
On routers, switches and servers an ACL applies rules to ports or IP addresses with the hosts or networks allowed to use them, for inbound and outbound traffic, much like a firewall.
Name-based network ACLs are a questionable idea because TCP, UDP and ICMP headers carry no domain names, so the enforcing device must resolve names itself, which adds attack surface.
ACLs are easy to understand but error-prone with a high maintenance cost; maintaining authorization data often costs as much administration as managing authentication credentials.
A minimal RBAC model is equivalent to an ACL whose only entries are groups, and modern SQL-based ACLs manage groups and inheritance in a hierarchy, so they can express all that RBAC expresses.

definition.text: A type of access control that restricts access to objects by the identity of subjects or the groups they belong to, where a subject with a permission can pass it on to others.

facts.text: DAC is discretionary because a subject holding a permission can pass it, perhaps indirectly, to any other subject, unless restrained by mandatory access control.

In the common owner-based implementation each object has an owner who controls its permissions and can make policy decisions; DAC is built on ACLs and the owner group's policy grants or restricts access.
The Unix file mode is a straightforward example, with read, write and execute bits for User, Group and Others; the Linux file system supports DAC.
Capability systems are a second implementation: subjects can transfer access, but not to just any subject, since the passer must already have access to the receiver, in line with least privilege.
A system can run MAC and DAC together, with DAC covering access that subjects can transfer among each other and MAC imposing constraints on it.
DAC is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the object's owner group has too much power.

definition.text: A type of access control in which a secured environment, such as an operating system or database, constrains a subject's ability to access or modify an object under a centrally set policy.

facts.text: Subjects and objects each carry security attributes; whenever a subject tries to access an object, the kernel checks the attributes and the policy in place and decides whether to grant access.

The policy is centrally controlled by a policy administrator and enforced for all users, who cannot override it or grant access to files that would otherwise be restricted, unlike DAC where users set policy.

MAC was traditionally tied to multilevel security and military systems, defined by TCSEC as access by an object's sensitivity label and the subject's clearance; SELinux, AppArmor and Windows Mandatory Integrity Control now bring it to mainstream systems.
MAC is strict and straightforward but not flexible; SELinux gives fine-grained control suited to high-security environments, at the cost of complexity and a steep learning curve.

title: Attribute-based access control

definition.text: An access control paradigm in which a subject's authorization to perform operations is decided by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and sometimes the environment.

facts.text: ABAC policy rules are Boolean functions of the subject's, the object's and the environment's attributes, so the only limits are the policy language and the availability of attributes.
Attributes fall into four categories: subject (age, clearance, department, role), action (read, delete, approve), object (type, department, classification, location) and contextual (time, location).

Unlike RBAC, ABAC expresses complex rule sets over many attributes and needs no explicit authorizations for individual subjects, reducing the work of managing access lists and groups; user-centric models ignore time of day or user IP.

A policy combines attributes into statements of what is allowed; it can grant or deny, be local or global, and override others, for example a user can edit a document if they own it and it is in draft mode.

The recommended architecture has a Policy Enforcement Point that protects the app and sends authorization requests, a Policy Decision Point that evaluates them against policies, and Policy Information Points that supply attributes from LDAP or databases.
XACML defines an architecture, a policy language and a request/response scheme for ABAC, as do ALFA and NIST's NGAC; attribute management is left to traditional IAM tools, databases and directories.

ABAC can protect API methods, such as allowing managers to approve transactions up to their approval limit, and databases with rules like a manager may SELECT a transaction if the user's region equals the transaction's region.

ABAC is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation hard, so the guide calls it not commonly used; more granular controls add performance overhead and affect the user experience.

notes: The ByteByteGo guide (ae72dcd324a9) says ABAC is not commonly used, while Wikipedia says adoption is spreading in government and military agencies (ddc292b90767, 1308c4ae2317); they describe different scopes, so it is not recorded as a conflict.

definition.text: An approach to restricting system access to authorized users, defined around roles and privileges rather than around individual users.

facts.text: Roles are created for job functions and permissions are assigned to roles; users get permissions only through their roles, so adding a user or changing a department means assigning the right roles.

RBAC has three rules: a subject can exercise a permission only with a selected or assigned role, the active role must be authorized for the subject, and the permission must be authorized for that role.

The model has subjects, roles, permissions and sessions, with many-to-many subject-to-role and permission-to-role assignment relations; a subject may have several simultaneous sessions in different roles.

Roles can form a hierarchy where higher-level roles subsume the permissions of sub-roles, and constraints can enforce separation of duties; the NIST/ANSI/INCITS standard adds these as hierarchical and constrained RBAC.

RBAC eases administration in large organizations with hundreds of users and thousands of permissions, is widely accepted as best practice within a single system, and is the mode Kubernetes offers, with each role listing allowed actions.
RBAC can implement DAC or MAC policies, and ABAC and relationship-based access control are models that build on it.

RBAC is criticized for role explosion when finer granularity is needed, becomes extremely complex across dozens of systems without hierarchical roles, and does not look at message context such as a connection's source.
An ACL grants or denies write access to a particular file without saying how it may change, whereas an RBAC permission is an operation, such as creating a credit account in a financial application.

definition.text: An XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS.

facts.text: XACML defines a declarative, fine-grained, attribute-based policy language, an architecture and a processing model for evaluating access requests against policies; it can also implement role-based access control.
A Policy Enforcement Point intercepts the user's request, converts it to an XACML authorization request and sends it to the Policy Decision Point, which evaluates it against its configured policies.

The PDP gets policies through a Policy Retrieval Point managed by a Policy Administration Point, fetches attributes from Policy Information Points, and returns Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate for the PEP to enforce.

Rules approve (Permit) or reject (Deny) a request, or give Indeterminate if their conditions fail to evaluate; rules group into policies, policies into larger policies, and a target decides whether a policy applies.
Combining algorithms, such as deny-unless-permit and permit-unless-deny, resolve conflicts when rules or policies contradict each other by merging their decisions into one final decision.
An obligation is a directive from the PDP to the PEP on what must happen before or after approval, such as logging; if the PEP cannot comply, access may not be realized, while advice may be ignored.

XACML specifies only the policy language, not the design of a PDP, and leaves attribute management to IAM tools, databases and directories; many PDPs use it, and Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source PDP.
XACML 3.0 added delegation, which supports decentralized administration by letting an authority hand all or part of its authority to another user without modifying the root policy.

title: Relationship-based access control
article: Role-based access control#Relation to other models > Relationship-based access control

definition.text: A model evolved from RBAC in which a subject's permission to access a resource is defined by the relationships between subjects and resources.

facts.text: In ReBAC a subject's permission to access a resource is defined by the presence of relationships between the subject and the resource.
It allows fine-grained permissions, for example in a social network where users share posts with other specific users.
ABAC attributes can be compared with one another to give relation-based control, and XACML conditions can implement relationship-based access control.

definition.text: A requirement that two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations, so no one individual can breach security through dual privilege.

facts.text: Separation of duties ensures that two or more people are involved in authorizing critical operations, so no individual can effect a breach of security through dual privilege.

By extension, no person may hold a role that exercises audit, control or review authority over another role held at the same time; the same person should not both create a login account and authorize its creation.
In RBAC, constraints that restrict permission inheritance from opposing roles achieve separation of duties, and RBAC is particularly well suited to it.
XACML conditions can implement segregation-of-duty checks.

title: Policy decision and enforcement points
article: rfc>2904#4. Relationship of Authorization and Policy > 4.4. Distributed Policy

definition.text: An authorization split into points: a policy is retrieved by a Policy Retrieval Point, evaluated at a Policy Decision Point and enforced at a Policy Enforcement Point.

facts.text: Each independent policy must be retrieved, evaluated and enforced; a PRP retrieves it from a policy repository, a PDP evaluates it and a PEP enforces it.

The PEP intercepts a user's request to a resource, asks the PDP whether access is approved or rejected, and acts on the answer; for example a NAS enforces destination address limits with filters and a router enforces QoS restrictions.
The PDP is the central, environment-independent point that evaluates requests against policies and makes the final access decision: Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate.
Policy Information Points hold the data policy conditions are evaluated against, such as resource status, session state or time of day; the PDP queries them for attribute values when needed.
Evaluation may need information not available where the policy was retrieved, so the evaluator must either query the remote administration for it or forward the policy to be evaluated there.
In an API, an interceptor asks the PDP whether a caller may perform an action; the PDP fetches the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only on Permit is the business logic called.
Any server in an authorization transaction may retrieve or evaluate a policy and any service equipment may enforce one; policy repositories may sit on those servers or elsewhere in the network.

definition.text: An architectural framework for understanding the authorization of Internet resources and services and for deriving requirements for authorization protocols.

facts.text: It assumes the parties have already been authenticated, and names four entities: the user, the user home organization that checks the user may have the service, the provider's AAA server, and the service equipment that delivers the service.

Authorization rests on chained bilateral agreements, user to home organization and home organization to provider; the request succeeds only if both are honored, and trust, for example through Kerberos or a certificate authority, makes each entity accept the policy.

In the agent sequence the AAA server applies policy and configures the service equipment; in pull the equipment asks the AAA server; in push the user first gets a ticket from the AAA server and presents it to the equipment.

When the user's home organization differs from the service provider, as in roaming, or several providers act in concert as in a distributed service, requests are chained through servers that rely on trust in one another.
